subject: environmental-science
title: Cycles & Systems: The Water Cycle
welcome_lead: Water keeps moving — sea to sky to land and back again.
meta_desc: KS3 environmental science: water cycle, evaporation, rain.
final_note: Every glass of water you drink has been around for billions of years.

concepts.def: Water turning from liquid to gas.

Water falling as rain, snow or hail.
Water flowing on the surface to rivers.
A repeating loop with no real start or end.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Sun heats oceans, rivers and puddles. Water evaporates into the air as invisible water vapour.
Up high it's cold. Vapour condenses into tiny droplets forming clouds. When droplets join they fall as precipitation — rain, snow or hail.
Some water soaks into the ground. The rest runs off into streams, rivers and back to the sea. Plants also release vapour through transpiration.

mcqs.q: What is the leading driver of global deforestation?
options: Forest fires alone.
Logging for timber and paper.
Agriculture (especially cattle ranching, soy, palm oil).

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils often nutrient-poor despite abundant vegetation?
options: Forest fires alone.
Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Rainforests have rich soils because they are productive.
Rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients cycle quickly through living biomass, not soil.

mcqs.q: Why are invasive species often more harmful than native species?
options: Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
They are larger than native species.
They lack natural predators or competitors in their new environment, so they spread unchecked.
They are inherently more aggressive than native species.
